content: Prolonged use of urinary catheters is a common practice in individuals requiring long-term care. However, this practice is associated with a significant risk of developing catheter-related urinary tract infections (UTIs) and other complications. Various types of urethral catheters are available, some of which are specifically designed to reduce the risk of infection. For instance, certain catheters are impregnated with antiseptic or antibiotic agents. In addition to infection prevention, factors such as ease of use, patient and caregiver comfort, and cost-effectiveness play a critical role in determining the choice of catheter. The primary aim of this study was to identify the most suitable type of indwelling urinary catheter for long-term bladder drainage in adults. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Incontinence Group Specialised Register, which includes databases such as CENTRAL and MEDLINE, as well as handsearching journals, conference proceedings, and reference lists of relevant articles. The search was last updated on March 31, 2011. The study included all randomized trials that compared different types of indwelling urinary catheters for long-term use, defined as catheterization lasting more than 30 days. Data extraction was performed independently by two reviewers, with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer. The analysis followed the guidelines outlined in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions. Three trials involving a total of 102 adults were included in the review. These trials were conducted in various settings and employed different study designs: two were parallel-group trials, and one was a randomized cross-over trial. The trials assessed only two of the six targeted comparisons: antiseptic-impregnated catheters versus standard catheters (one trial) and one type of standard catheter versus another standard catheter (two trials). The single small cross-over trial evaluating silver alloy (antiseptic) impregnated catheters was insufficient to determine their effectiveness. Similarly, the two trials comparing different types of standard catheters yielded imprecise results due to small sample sizes, resulting in wide confidence intervals that could not exclude clinically significant differences. However, one trial suggested that hydrogel-coated latex catheters might be better tolerated than silicone catheters, as indicated by a lower risk of early removal (risk ratio [RR] 0.41, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.22 to 0.77). The updated search did not identify any additional evidence. Overall, very few trials have compared different types of catheters for long-term bladder drainage, and the available studies were small and methodologically weak. Consequently, the evidence is insufficient to draw reliable practical conclusions. Further high-quality trials are urgently needed to address this critical gap in evidence for a clinically significant issue.
